comments.text: I was just thinking about this quite recently, so this video is quite timely. In my thought experiment, I was thinking about bank tellers as well. What I came to conclude is that bank tellers are not a very good proxy for other types of jobs simply because their roles were uniquely mutable. For example, in the past, the primary function of a bank teller was to receive and distribute cash and process check deposits. With the advent of direct deposit and the internet, one might have expected cash and checks to disappear. However, that was not the case, as the cultural habit of using cash did not go away. Many workers continued to be paid in cash, and many businesses continued to receive cash payments and needed to deposit them. Many of these workers and businesses likely resisted changing their habits. Sure, some banks could have eliminated all bank tellers to "save" money, but doing so would have alienated those customers, giving a competitive advantage to banks that retained human tellers. Further, the mutability of the role stems from the fact that customers often have questions about other bank products (e.g., loans, wealth management, etc.), and bank tellers can use their freed-up time to act as quasi-secretaries who answer questions and direct customers to the appropriate person within the bank. This mutability is primarily a function of humans' resistance to change and the role being customer-facing. I suspect there will be other roles that persist longer than necessary because people trust only humans to perform the task or because of regulatory barriers (e.g., lawyers or doctors). However, there are many roles where this inherent mutability does not exist. If your entire job is to crunch numbers and write standardized reports, then AI can likely already do your job, and for less money. Those types of roles, which involve little to no customer interaction and face no meaningful regulatory barriers (e.g., some accounting work), are much more likely to be eliminated if AI can perform them better.
